analysis.one_liner: Stops carmakers from selling your vehicle's data and gives you free control over it.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on December 18, 2024 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it died with no vote as the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Modern cars constantly record where you go and how you drive. This bill would forbid manufacturers from selling or sharing that data — including with foreign governments like China, Russia, and Iran — unless a court order, emergency, or the owner's consent allows it. It would also require automakers to give owners free access to their own vehicle's data through a standard interface, with FTC-enforced rules and standards. The bill never got a hearing or a vote before the congressional session ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Vehicle owners — drivers of cars, trucks, and farm and construction equipment. Today, connected cars record location, driving behavior, and in-car activity, and manufacturers can sell or share that data. The bill would require the owner's explicit, written, revocable consent before a manufacturer could access it, bar sales except under court order or in emergencies, prohibit sharing Americans' personal data with China, Russia, North Korea, Iran, and Venezuela, and guarantee owners free access to and deletion of their own data through a secure, technology-neutral interface.

how_it_helps.text: Bans manufacturers from selling, leasing, or sharing vehicle data except under a warrant, a court order with notice and a hearing, an emergency, or the owner's explicit permission.
Prohibits sharing any American's personally identifiable information — including location and internet activity — with China, Russia, North Korea, Iran, or Venezuela.
Requires manufacturers to give owners free, unrestricted access to their vehicle's data through a secure, technology-neutral interface, with no fees or proprietary devices required.
Requires open APIs so owners can delete their own data and control vehicle settings, and directs the FTC to set and periodically update security standards.
Makes violations enforceable by the FTC as unfair or deceptive practices.

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, who would lose a growing revenue stream from selling vehicle data and would have to build open, standards-based data interfaces for owners. Some compliance costs could ultimately be passed on in vehicle prices.

drawbacks.text: Section 7 preempts any state or federal law touching the same requirements, which would override stronger state auto-privacy protections in places like California.

The bill lets manufacturers access operator data without consent whenever it is 'solely to improve covered vehicle performance or safety' — a broad exception that could swallow much of the consent rule in practice.
Compliance costs for automakers would be significant: building open, technology-neutral data interfaces and complying with new FTC standards, costs that could be passed to buyers.
The FTC must write detailed technical standards within roughly 21 months and must do so with no new appropriations, which could delay or weaken implementation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are substantial: your car's data would stop being a product sold about you, and you would own access to it. The costs are real but modest: compliance work for manufacturers, and the FTC would need to write standards without new money. The bill is also somewhat blunt — its preemption clause would wipe out any state auto-data privacy law, and its safety-research exception is broad enough that manufacturers could still access data without consent by labeling it performance or safety work. On balance, though, it addresses a fast-growing privacy problem in a fairly direct way.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the final two weeks of the congressional session and sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee, which never acted on it before the session ended.

narrative.text: Introduced December 18, 2024, less than three weeks before the 118th Congress expired.
Referred the same day to the House Energy and Commerce Committee; no hearing, markup, or floor vote followed.
The Congress ended January 3, 2025, and the bill expired with the session, carrying over no further action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers keep full control over the data their connected cars generate and the revenue it can bring, and owners gained no new rights.

for.name: Rep. Andy Biggs
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no action — no hearing, markup, or report before the Congress ended.

against.name: Automobile manufacturers
against.what_they_did: The industry has long opposed restrictions on collecting and monetizing vehicle telematics data and on right-to-repair access requirements.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never attracted enough action to reveal a partisan divide: one Republican sponsor, one cosponsor, and no votes or committee activity.

industries.note: They would lose the ability to collect, monetize, and gate access to the data their connected vehicles generate, and would have to build open data interfaces at their own expense. Their interest in blocking this runs against vehicle owners' control over their own data.
A secondary market in vehicle location and behavior data would be sharply curtailed, since sharing would require the owner's explicit consent or legal process.

industries.industry: Independent repair shops and aftermarket device makers
industries.note: The technology-neutral access requirement would let owners authorize third parties to read vehicle data without paying manufacturer licensing fees, weakening a closed ecosystem.
